Graph layout for ontologies

Tidy Stress and Mycelium

Executive summary

Tidy Stress and Mycelium are two new layouts for ontology diagrams, built so that a reader follows each link to the right class. Tidy Stress suits the 10 to 30 classes of a typical ontology; Mycelium suits large and hub-heavy ones. Best Read, the auto mode, runs both and keeps the more readable drawing. A clean-up and a link routing then run after the layout, and both also work after any other layout. The package is plain JavaScript with no dependencies, under the Apache 2.0 licence.

  • Value: Best Read draws about half the crossed links and an eighth of the links through classes of the best tuned open-source layouts. Its drawings stay compact (a median of 6.3 times the area of the class boxes) and take under a second. The same methods grow a drawing click by click as a reader explores, without moving the classes already shown, and can draw hierarchies top-down (an experiment for now).
  • Benchmark scope: 11 open-source layouts (Graphviz neato, fdp and sfdp; ELK stress, force and layered; WebCola; d3-force; dagre; Cytoscape cose and fcose), each at general settings and tuned for its best chance. They were run on 15 development graphs of 13 to 179 classes and on 36 graphs never seen during development: held-out graphs, eight published ontologies and graphs from the Rome benchmark. Every ranking uses five measures, pictured below.
  • Results: Best Read ranks first of 12 at general and at tuned settings, and again on the 36 unseen graphs. Others lead on some things: some layouts draw smaller by letting links run through classes, Graphviz is faster, WebCola keeps graph distances more faithfully, and d3-force does better above 3,000 classes, even when Best Read runs seven times as long as d3-force.
  • Also in the package: an interactive Layout Lab, and a method for working with an AI assistant to turn a person's sense of a good drawing into code.

An ontology diagram is only useful if a reader can follow each link from one class to another. Five problems get in the way, pictured below. The two that matter most are links that cross, and links that pass under a class box, so that two unrelated classes look connected. Then come links that cross at a shallow angle, links that leave a class almost together, and a drawing that sprawls over far more canvas than its classes need. General-purpose layouts reduce crossings only as a side effect and do little about links under boxes. Tidy Stress and Mycelium are built to minimize both, without letting the drawing sprawl.

What we value, and what we deliberately do not. These layouts are for ontologies, not for graphs in general, and that decides which measures count. All rankings on this page use these five:

  • Crossed links and links through classes come first. Each can make a reader follow the wrong link.
  • Crossing angle and angular resolution come next. A shallow crossing is harder to follow than a square one, and links that leave a class in almost the same direction are hard to tell apart.
  • Area matters, but less than all four.

Two common measures are left out on purpose: how faithfully drawn distance follows graph distance (normalized stress), and how even the link lengths are. A business ontology often joins several domains, such as sales, finance and operations, each linked back to shared classes like Person or Organization. Drawing every related class close would pull the domains into each other; keeping each domain together, even when that makes a link to a shared class long, is the point. Length and distance are therefore not goals here, and the main rankings leave them out. Readers who value them, or a top-down hierarchy, can add them with the tabs above each ranking table; our layouts do poorly on distance and length. (For models where the hierarchy is the content, see Top-down hierarchies.) Measured over the 51 graphs: normalized stress is 0.085 after the stress placement alone, 0.132 after Tidy Stress's search, 0.146 for Best Read and 0.159 after the clean-up and the routing. Global distances are therefore about half as faithful. Local closeness is not lost: the share of a class's linked classes that are among its nearest classes is 55.8% after the stress placement and 55.6% at the end. A reader can still take nearness as linked; they should not read a long distance as unrelated.

Below, a 179-class banking ontology: eleven class hierarchies joined by relationships. On the left is the open-source layout with the fewest crossed links plus links through classes on this ontology; on the right, ours. Mark problems shows every crossing (dot) and every link that runs through a class (red).

Two layouts and an auto mode that keeps the better drawing; the clean-up and routing work after any layout

Tidy Stress up to a few dozen classes

Places classes so that straight-line distances match how many links apart they are, then tidies the drawing: it moves classes to remove crossings, to take them off links that run through them, and to shorten long links, keeping a move only if nothing else gets worse.

Mycelium large and hub-heavy ontologies

Draws groups of closely linked classes as compact pods joined by longer threads. Every hub gets a ring wide enough for all its neighbors, and classes with a single link fan out around the class they hang from, with room for the link's label.

Top-down hierarchies, on request

The same placement with every subclass at least 40 px below its superclass, then the clean-up and its finishing passes, which keep it that way. For models where the hierarchy is the content. It draws a third to a half of the crossings of tuned ELK layered, the usual choice for top-down drawings. An experiment for now, not yet among the entry points; see Top-down.

Link routing after any layout

Draws the links on the final positions: parallel and reciprocal links as arcs side by side, self-links as loops on the most open side, links still running through a class bent round it inside the drawing, link ends spread along the side of a crowded class, and link names placed on or beside their link where they cover nothing; a class that a link still runs through is pushed off it when that helps. See Link routing.

Clean-up after any layout

Fixes what is left the way a person does: moves a class off a link into nearby open space, turns leaves and small groups that hang from one class until their links are clear, and spreads the regions where problems pile up. It uses what is left of 1.5 s, at most half a second. See Clean-up after the layout.

Best Read runs both layouts and keeps the more readable drawing

Best Read chooses between the two layouts for a given ontology: it runs Tidy Stress and Mycelium, scores both drawings for readability, keeps the better one, and cleans it up. Above 100 classes it runs Mycelium alone: at that size Mycelium drew far fewer crossings and links through classes in every test, and running both would double the time. It changes no setting inside either layout; it only chooses between their results, by crossed links, links through classes, near misses, overlaps, mean link length and area.

On a typical small ontology, Tidy Stress draws no crossing and no link through a class

Most ontologies people draw have 10 to 30 classes. There the open-source layouts are already decent, and the difference is in the details: fewer crossings and no link through a class.

On hub-heavy ontologies, Mycelium gives each hub room so its links stop running through other classes

A 53-class clinical record in which three classes link to almost everything. No placement can untangle this fully. Mycelium gives each hub a ring of room so that its links stop running through other classes, at the cost of a larger drawing.

Best Read ranks first of 12 layouts, with about half the crossings of the best tuned open-source layouts

Each layout is ranked on each of the 15 development graphs (13 to 179 classes) on the five measures, and the places are averaged over the graphs: 1 is best and lower is better, and layouts with equal results share a place. In the tables each measure's column is that average place, and the overall score is the average of the five; the Place column orders the layouts by that score. The open-source layouts are given their best chance. Each library tried several settings and seeds, its default run included, and kept the run with the fewest crossed links plus links through classes, the two counts we lead on. The settings are listed under Benchmark method. Layered layouts were given subclass links oriented parent to child. Ours appear with the clean-up.

The main table ranks Best Read, the auto mode a user would call, against the eleven open-source layouts. Best Read always draws with one of our two layouts, so ranking all three together would count our drawings twice; the second table ranks Tidy Stress and Mycelium each on its own against the same eleven. The tabs add optional measures for readers who value them.

Against tuned open-source layouts, Best Read ranks first on the five measures, with an overall score of 2.9 (its average place; lower is better), against 4.8 for the next, tuned WebCola. It draws 452 crossed links and 39 links through classes over the 15 graphs; the closest open-source layout, tuned neato, draws 960 and 81, in about 16 times the area.

Ours lead on the two problems that mislead a reader

  • Crossed links: 452 for Best Read, against 960 for tuned neato, 971 for tuned WebCola and 1,070 for tuned sfdp.
  • Links through classes: 39 for Best Read, against 307 for tuned WebCola. Tuned neato draws 81, in about 16 times the area: its median drawing is 104 times the area of its boxes, against Best Read's 6.3.
  • Every graph: Best Read has the fewest crossed links plus links through classes, or ties for the fewest, on all 15 development graphs and on all 36 graphs never seen during development.
  • Angles: Tidy Stress ranks first on crossing angle and Best Read narrowly first on angular resolution.
  • After tuning: tuning brought the open-source layouts closer (WebCola, sfdp and neato draw 13%, 17% and 34% fewer crossings tuned than at general settings), and the lead holds.

Others lead on area, speed and faithful distances

  • Area: Cytoscape cose, dagre and fcose draw tighter, cose and dagre by letting links run through boxes (4,092 and 1,330 of them).
  • Time: Best Read takes 0.5 s at the median; Graphviz at general settings takes tens of milliseconds. See Time and scale.
  • Distance and even lengths: with those two measures added (third tab), WebCola ranks first and Best Read second; Mycelium, which lets links between groups run long on purpose, falls to fifth.
  • Very large graphs: at 3,335 classes d3-force draws fewer problems. See Very large graphs.

Taken together. On the five measures, Best Read places first of twelve, with an overall score (average place) of 2.9 against 4.8 for the next, tuned WebCola. That gap is mostly the two counts that make a reader follow the wrong link: about half the crossings and an eighth of the links through classes of the nearest contenders. The others lead where a drawing can be smaller or faster by letting those problems stand. Which measures matter most is a judgment backed by Purchase's studies of crossings, not by a study of our own (see Limits).

The lead holds on 36 graphs never seen during development

The layouts and the clean-up were developed on the 15 graphs above, so their lead there could partly be fitted to those graphs. To check, they were run, unchanged, on 36 graphs that were never viewed or used for tuning: ten held-out graphs in shapes the development graphs do not cover (18 to 304 classes), eight published ontologies (FOAF, Dublin Core terms, OWL-Time, DCAT 3, BFO 2020, DOLCE+DnS Ultralite, SAREF core and GoodRelations) and 18 graphs of the Rome collection, the classic graph-drawing benchmark (20 to 100 nodes). Same open-source layouts and tuned settings, same measures. All but the two largest can be opened in the explorer below.

The lead holds. Over the 36 graphs, Best Read draws 1,565 crossed links and 138 links through classes, against 2,160 and 212 for tuned neato (in nearly ten times the area), 2,429 and 780 for tuned WebCola, and 2,411 and 601 for tuned sfdp. It places first of twelve with an overall score (average place) of 3.0, ahead of tuned neato (4.6) and WebCola (4.8).

These graphs also caught a fault the development graphs had hidden. On the published ontologies and the Rome graphs, Mycelium alone drew fewer crossings than Best Read, because Best Read chose with a score that also penalized long links and passed over Mycelium's pod layouts. It now chooses without those penalties. That change was decided on the 15 development graphs (6.5% fewer crossed links plus links through classes, 7% more area) and only then measured here: 1,297 → 1,284 crossings and 134 → 108 links through classes on the public graphs.

On the 36 unseen graphs Best Read still ranks first, with an overall score of 3.0 against 4.6 for tuned neato (average place; lower is better), so the lead is not fitted to the development graphs.

Top-down, every subclass link points down, with a third to a half of the crossings of ELK layered

Tidy Stress, Mycelium and Best Read are built for conceptual ontologies, where classes are joined mostly by relationships. There a subclass link is one relationship among many, and about half of them point down. For a taxonomy, or any model where the hierarchy is the content, a reader rightly expects general classes above specific ones. A reviewer called the first stance a defect for such models, and we agree.

The same methods draw hierarchies top-down. The placement is the same stress placement, with every subclass at least 40 px below its superclass: the constraints are applied by projection after each placement sweep, in the spirit of Dwyer, Koren and Marriott's constrained stress majorization (IPSep-CoLa, 2006). Every tidy-up move and leaf placement must keep them. The clean-up and its finishing passes then run in a top-down mode, where no move may lift a subclass to less than 20 px below its superclass. Best Read, top-down, chooses between the two layouts drawn that way, as Best Read does.

The usual tools for top-down drawings are layered layouts: ELK layered and dagre, given subclass links oriented parent to child and tuned as in the rankings. On the development graphs they and WebCola were given only runs that keep subclass links top-down; on the unseen graphs, the tuned runs. Totals:

Drawn top-down, Best Read points every subclass link down and draws a third to a half of tuned ELK layered's crossings and a quarter to an eighth of its links through classes, on every set of graphs.

Every subclass link points down, with a third to a half of the crossings of tuned ELK layered (588 against 1,663 on the development graphs, 420 against 1,433 and 1,391 against 3,100 on the graphs never seen during development) and between a quarter and an eighth of its links through classes (141 against 516, 63 against 509, 135 against 751). The layered layouts keep a strict layering, which costs crossings on ontologies whose relationships cut across the hierarchy, and even then they leave some subclass links pointing up or sideways. dagre packs tighter by letting many more links run through classes. WebCola with the same constraints comes closest on the development graphs, in twice the area and about 40 times the time.

The cost of going top-down, against Best Read's usual drawing: on the development graphs, 30% more crossed links and about three and a half times the links through classes (588 and 141 against 452 and 39), most of it on broad taxonomies and hub-heavy graphs. On the public graphs it costs much less: 10% more crossed links and 36 more links through classes. Area grows by a fifth to two fifths.

Status. The top-down drawing is an experiment for now: it runs in the benchmark code (tools/layout-bench/engines3.js and topdown.mjs), on top of the library's own functions, and is not yet one of the library's entry points. The clean-up's top-down mode is in the library.

The Tree. The library also has a tidy tree (_ogTreeLayout), after Reingold and Tilford (1981). Classes stand on levels, each one level below its deepest superclass, and each level sits deep enough that no line from a parent to a child clips a sibling. The tree itself therefore has no crossing and no link through a class. Real taxonomies are not trees, though: second superclasses and relationships cut across it. With them it draws two to four times the crossings of the top-down stress drawing and from four to over a hundred times the links through classes, on every set above. A tree is the better picture only for a model that is nearly a pure tree.

Other ways tried, before the top-down drawing above:

  • A soft hierarchy term in the placement, as the review suggested (a penalty λ·max(0, yparent − ychild + δ)² added to stress, in the spirit of Dwyer and Koren's DIG-CoLa, 2005), was tested two ways. As a partial correction after each placement sweep, on eight development graphs before the clean-up, it turned 94% of subclass links down but raised crossed links from 203 to 262 and links through classes from 91 to 166. As a true term of the stress energy, minimized by the same majorization (each violated subclass link adds a target height to its class's update, as DIG-CoLa does), it hardly changed direction: even at λ = 16, over the 15 graphs, the share pointing down rose only from 46% to 54%, with 14% more links through classes, because the tidy-up and the placement of one-link classes that follow decide most directions, and making them keep the hierarchy is the hard version measured below. Reflecting a child below its parent instead of pressing it flat, so that a parent's children keep their fan, did no better (332 and 190). In the clean-up, keeping every subclass at least 20 px below raised crossed links 27% and links through classes fourfold over the 15 graphs; even as a small tie-breaker it raised links through classes from 55 to 67.
  • Choosing the tree automatically. Best Read used to draw the tree as well when at least half the links were subclass links, and keep it when it had no crossed link and no link through a class in at most 1.5 times the area. Over the 51 graphs it was chosen once, on Dublin Core terms, where the other drawing has no problem either, so it was dropped.

Readers who value a top-down hierarchy can also rank every layout by it: the ranking tables have a tab that adds it as a sixth measure.

When a drawing grows, the classes already shown stay put and the new ones are placed cleanly

A diagram is rarely drawn once. A modeller adds classes, and a reader of a graph browser clicks a class to see its neighbours. Each time, redrawing from scratch would move the classes the reader already knows. These layouts can keep the earlier drawing and place only what is new.

Exploring a graph: each click draws a third of the crossings of a force-directed expansion, and moves nothing

A graph browser usually starts from one class or a small part of a model, and each click adds a class's hidden neighbours. To measure that, simulated sessions were run on 12 of the test graphs, two starts each (one class, or a class and its neighbourhood) and two seeds. That gave 48 sessions of up to 8 clicks, each click adding up to 15 classes: 425 drawings in all, every link drawn straight. Each click was drawn four ways:

  • A typical force-directed expansion: d3-force with the classes already shown pinned, and the new ones started beside the clicked class. The settings are a 170 px link distance, repulsion −300, collision on the boxes and 300 ticks. This is the usual way graph browsers grow a drawing.
  • Keep, exact: draw(…, { keep, exact: true }). Nothing already drawn moves.
  • Keep: draw(…, { keep }). The clean-up may also move earlier classes a little.
  • Redraw: draw from scratch at every click.

Keeping the drawing exactly (nothing moves) gives a third of the crossings and a fifth of the links through classes of a typical force-directed expansion, in half the time.

Each click drawn byCrossed links per drawingLinks through classesNames over a class or nameEarlier classes movedTime per click, mean
Typical force-directed expansion71.725.76.3none12 ms
Keep, exact24.95.41.9none6 ms
Keep20.01.11.22.7% of the drawing132 ms
Redraw13.31.61.138.5% of the drawing237 ms

With nothing moving, each click draws a third of the crossings, a fifth of the links through classes and a third of the covered names of the force-directed expansion, in half the time. The mean time includes the first drawing of each session, which is a full layout of up to 15 classes; the clicks after it take a few milliseconds. Three things make the difference:

  • New classes that link only to the clicked class go on an arc round it, on its most open side, on one ring or two, with subclasses together. The arc is kept only when it scores better than placing them one at a time.
  • Every other new class goes where it causes the fewest crossings and links through classes, rather than where forces balance.
  • The placement sees each pair of linked classes once, so data graphs with a dozen links between the same two classes stay quick.

A redraw is cleaner still but moves the earlier classes by over a third of the drawing, so the reader loses their place. Allowing small moves (keep without exact) almost removes links through classes, but earlier classes move 2.7% of the drawing on average. That suits a "tidy" command better than every click. With the link routing instead of straight links, keep-exact leaves 20.7 crossed links and 1.0 link through a class per drawing: the bends take most of the rest off the classes, for about 25 ms per click.

How to call it from a graph browser

  1. The first view: draw(boxes, links). A single class works, so an exploration can start from one.
  2. Each click: append the new classes and their links, then call draw(boxes, links, { keep, exact: true }), with the earlier positions in keep and null for each new class.
  3. A "tidy" button: the same call without exact. Classes move a little, and links through classes nearly disappear.
  4. A "redraw" button, for when the picture has grown far from its first shape: draw(boxes, links).
  5. Straight links: where links that bend round classes would confuse, add route: { straight: true }. No link is then bent round a class; repeated and reciprocal links between two classes are still arcs side by side, and self-links loops. Add arcs: false as well to draw repeated links as parallel straight lines.
  6. Drag: a class the reader has dragged stays where they put it if its position goes into keep with exact: true.

After an edit, keeping the old positions costs some crossings; redrawing moves every class

Redrawing a model after an edit moves the classes a reader already knows: with 10% more classes, a redraw moves the old ones by about a third of the drawing's diagonal on average (25 graphs). draw(…, { keep }) takes the earlier positions, with null for each new class. It places the new classes round the classes they link to, then lets the clean-up and the routing make local moves. With exact: true no old class moves at all, which suits a drawing arranged by hand. Over the 15 development and 10 held-out graphs:

Keeping the old positions costs 18 to 22% more crossed links than a redraw, but a redraw moves the old classes by 30% of the diagonal.

Classes addedDrawingCrossed linksLinks through classesOld classes movedMean time
3% (54)keep, exact83444none26 ms
keep807182.3% of the diagonal219 ms
redraw6851330%453 ms

Keeping costs crossings, because the new links have to cross a picture that was not made for them; redrawing from time to time remains the way to a clean drawing. These numbers are the hard case: the added classes were picked at random, hubs included, where an edit usually adds a few classes in one place.

The clean-up removes two thirds of the links through classes, after any layout

Both layouts place classes by a global rule: stress, pods, hub rings. What a global rule leaves behind is local: a leaf sitting on a line, a corner where five links cross, a class that could step two box-widths aside into empty space. A person sees these at a glance and fixes them in a minute. The clean-up does the same automatically. It was taught by a person who explained how they do it (see How the clean-up was learned), in two rounds, and it runs in two parts:

  1. The clean-up proper came from Brendan tidying drawings by hand: single moves into open space, turning what hangs off one class, spreading crowded regions and moving groups.
  2. The finishing passes came from a second round: he watched the first part work, step by step, in the Layout Playback and named what was still wrong in a few words. "Don't fence me in", "push it off the line" and "pull it in from the edge" each became a short pass that runs after it.

Over the 15 test graphs, before and after the clean-up (totals; area is the drawing's bounding box divided by the total area of the class boxes). In each cell the value before the arrow is without the clean-up and the bold value after it is with the clean-up. Crossed links, links through classes, area and time are lower-is-better, so a lower value right of the arrow means the clean-up improved the drawing; the two angle measures are higher-is-better.

The clean-up takes Best Read's links through classes from 124 to 39, removes 7% of its crossed links and makes the drawing about a fifth smaller, for about 0.25 s more at the median.

LayoutCrossed links, totalLinks through classes, totalMean crossing angleMean angular resolutionMedian areaMedian time
Tidy Stress599 → 604299 → 13072° → 74°0.43 → 0.436.5 → 6.3159 ms → 435 ms
Mycelium455 → 450149 → 4962° → 66°0.43 → 0.4411.5 → 8.778 ms → 372 ms
Best Read484 → 452124 → 3970° → 72°0.45 → 0.448.0 → 6.3233 ms → 481 ms

Links through classes fall by two thirds (Best Read 124 → 39). Crossings fall a little (Best Read draws 7% fewer), crossing angles get slightly squarer, and the drawing gets smaller (Best Read's area 8.0 → 6.3 times its boxes, from pulling sprawling parts and groups in from the edge). The cost is time: Best Read's median rises from 0.2 to 0.5 s. The clean-up takes whatever is left of the time limit after the layout, at most a third of it, and is skipped when less than a fifteenth is left (these figures were measured at a 1.5 s limit, where that third is half a second; the default is 0.75 s since 12 November 2026). Above 100 classes the layout is given 40% of the limit so that the clean-up keeps its third: on large graphs that gives fewer problems than a longer layout. To fit in that time, the clean-up looks only at the links and classes near each move, through a grid of cells one link long, with the same results as checking every pair.

Worked example: every step of the clean-up on two graphs

Both parts, step by step, each walk-through on one graph from start to finish: a 115-class biomedical taxonomy drawn by Best Read, and a graph of a very different shape never seen during development, two big hubs that share many classes. The steps follow the order a person works in: look at the whole drawing, find the worst region, make room there, then make the easy fixes. Not every step has work to do on every graph; a step that changes nothing on the chosen graph is greyed out, and its tooltip says why. Each step has two tabs: the reasoning in plain terms, and the same step as the code computes it. ← → step through.

Walk through
The clean-up Finishing passes

Before fixing anything, look at the whole drawing with an imaginary grid over it. Where is the drawing, and where is the empty canvas inside its rectangle? Open space (green) is a resource: it is where classes can go to solve problems.

Then look at where the problems are: red dots are crossings, red links run through a class. They are not spread evenly. They cluster where the drawing is crowded, and one crowded spot often causes several at once: a leaf with no room near its parent ends up further away, crossing links on the way.

Let L̃ be the median link length. The open-space grid has cells of side 0.3 L̃ (here 45 px) over the bounding box. A cell is open when no class box, grown by a clearance c = 8 px, overlaps it and no link passes through it (links are sampled every third of a cell).

A crossing is a pair of links without a shared end whose straight segments intersect (orientation test). A link through a class is a link uv whose segment meets the box of a third class w grown by c (Liang–Barsky clipping). A class is cramped when the smallest angle between its links is under 15°; a crossing is sharp under 30°.

Count the problems in each cell of a coarser grid, one link long. The cells with the most problems (orange) form the region most in need of fixing; its center of gravity is the mean position of its problems.

Around that center, cut the space into eight pizza slices (dashed). Each slice is judged by how much open or sparse space lies just beyond the crowd in its direction (the shading): that is where there is room to push.

A crowded part of the drawing with no problem in it is left alone. Dense is fine when it reads well.

Problem points: the crossing point of a crossing, the center of the class a link runs through. On cells of side L̃, n(cell) counts problem points. Hot cells have n ≥ max(2, ⌈max n / 2⌉); regions are 8-connected groups of hot cells, ranked by Σn.

Center c = mean of the region's problem points; radius r₀ = min(1.5 L̃, maxi |pi − c| + 0.6 L̃). Slice k = 0…7 covers angles [−π + kπ/4, −π + (k+1)π/4).

Density ρ on cells of side L̃/2: 1 per class center and ¼ per link passing through, mean ρ̄. Room in slice k: Σ over cells at distance r₀ … r₀ + 2L̃ of max(0, ρ̄ − ρ) + ½·[ρ = 0].

Move every class in the region away from the center: further for classes near the region's edge, and further in slices with more room beyond them. Classes just outside are pushed too, less the further out they are, so the push makes room without piling a new crowd at the edge.

The push alone fixes nothing here: the counts are unchanged. It only makes room, which is why it is never judged on its own.

For a class at p in slice k with d = |p − c| < 3r₀:

p′ = p + a · L̃ · wk · f(d) · (p − c) / d

with f(d) = d / r₀ inside the region and max(0, 1 − (d − r₀) / 2r₀) beyond it, and wk = 1 (even) or 0.3 + 0.7 · roomk / max room (weighted by room). Six candidates, a ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.8} × the two weightings; the one with the lowest cost goes on to the repair.

With room made, a few single moves repair the region: a class at the end of a crossed link, or one a link runs through, moves into nearby open space. The spread is kept only if, after these repairs, the drawing is better than before it; otherwise everything goes back.

Then the easy fixes. A leaf, a short chain of leaves or a leaf triangle hangs off one class, so it can always be turned around that class until its links are clear. A leaf left on a line is a sign that a step was missed, not that the drawing is hard. A long label goes beside its neighbor rather than above or below, because a long label reads best on a link that runs sideways.

Here the repairs after the spread take links through classes from 10 to 7, remove the sharp crossing and add one crossing. The rest of the clean-up (three smaller spreads, three single moves and four leaf units) takes links through classes to 1. The figure shows the end, with arrows from the drawing right after the push.

Cost F = 6·crossings + 3·sharp crossings + 10·links through classes + 1·cramped classes + 1000·overlapping boxes + 600·max(0, A/A₀ − 1), with A the bounding-box area and A₀ its value before the clean-up. Link length has no term. A move is costed locally, over the links and classes it touches.

Repair: up to 4 greedy single moves among the classes in problems within 1.5r₀ + L̃ of c, each trying 16 nudges (8 directions × 0.1 and 0.25 L̃) and the 12 nearest open cells within 1.8 L̃. The spread is kept when F falls by more than 0.5.

Leaf units: for each class a, the parts of the graph cut off by removing a (a cut vertex) with at most 4 classes. Candidates: 24 turns about a × mirror × orderings (up to 3 classes); a single leaf also at 1, 1.6 and 2.4 times its distance, sideways directions first when its label is over 100 px wide; then sizes 0.75–2.8 at ±7.5°. A move is kept when F falls.

The taxonomy after the clean-up proper. One link still runs through a class (red).

The first pass is the simplest. When two classes hang off the same class by one link each, they can trade places. A long name beside a link that passes close by is the usual case: the shorter box fits where the longer one was in the way.

Here Influenza and Malaria trade places. The link from Malaria to InfectiousDisease passed within 9 px of Influenza, the margin drawn links keep (tick Before this step to see it, dashed amber); after the trade it is clear. The counts, taken with a 6 px margin, do not change.

For every pair of one-link classes a, b of the same class, swap their positions. Keep the swap when the cost of the problems involving them falls by more than 0.5 and neither box comes within 4 px of another. Cost: 6 per crossing and 10 per link through a class, with a 9 px margin, as the drawing is measured after the link routing.

"Don't fence me in." A one-link class whose link still crosses another link or runs through a class is boxed in by lines, often with open space round its neighbor. It looks there for the spot with the fewest problems, then the most room, then the shortest link.

"Push it off the line." A class that a link still runs through, or passes very close to, moves sideways off the line, just far enough. Or, when the link ends at a one-link class, that end turns a little round its neighbor. Each move is kept only if the problems involving the class fall.

Fence: candidates round the neighbor in 48 directions, from just clear of its box out to three link lengths, in steps of 30 px. Candidate c scores 200·x(c) − room(c) + 0.2·r. Here x counts 6 per crossing and 10 per link through a class (9 px margin), room is the clearance to the nearest box or link (capped at 120 px), and r is the distance to the neighbor. A candidate is taken only if x falls.

Push: a class within 9 px of a link moves along the link's normal by the distance need that clears it, or by 2·need. Otherwise a one-link end turns round its neighbor by ±8, ±15 or ±30°. A move is kept only if the class's problems fall by more than 0.5 and it overlaps nothing. Up to three rounds; both passes stop after 120 ms of the work clock.

"Pull it in from the edge." A chain or a small tree that hangs off the rest by one link and sprawls into empty canvas could fold up or down instead. Groups with an empty middle between them could sit closer. Use the open space inside the drawing before making the canvas bigger.

So a part that hangs by one link turns round the class it hangs from, or draws in toward it, and whole groups slide toward the middle. Parts nearest the edge go first. A move is kept only if the drawing gets smaller with no more problems.

Here 19 classes fold in, and the drawing narrows from 2,153 × 1,625 to 2,061 × 1,625 px, about 4% less area, with no new crossing or link through a class.

A part is what one class cuts off from the rest (a one-link class, a chain, a small tree), up to 40% of the classes. It turns round that class by up to 180° and/or draws in toward it, to 85, 70 or 55% of its reach. Whole groups (Louvain communities of four or more) slide toward the middle in one of 16 directions, by 40 to 640 px.

A move is taken only if all of these hold:

  • the problems involving the part do not rise (6 per crossing, 10 per link through a class);
  • no box comes within 14 px of another (40 px between groups);
  • no drawn-in link leaves less than 70 px between its two boxes, so its name has room;
  • the bounding box shrinks by more than 1%, or, with the box unchanged, the part's links get at least 25% shorter.

At most 100 ms of the work clock goes to parts, and 200 ms to the pass in all.

Single moves into open space do most of the work; each other step adds a little

In the layouts the clean-up runs in rounds, each round in this order, until nothing improves, the time is up, or a tenth of a second of work has passed without a kept move (late moves were rare and small, so this makes drawings about 8% faster with the same measures):

  1. Single moves: each class in a problem tries nearby open cells and small nudges.
  2. Leaf units turned around their anchor.
  3. Region spreading, as in the example, for the six regions with the most problems.
  4. Group moves: for each problem left, the classes on one side of the problem line, picked by position rather than by their links, move together away from it, with up to 4 repair moves; kept only if the drawing ends up better.

A last pass over leaf units and single classes follows, because the group moves can leave a leaf on a line. A class or problem that could not be improved is tried again only once something near it has moved.

After the finishing passes, one more tidy step: classes with no link, and small parts of the graph not linked to the rest, that sit among the classes of the main graph move out to one side of it, so that they neither crowd it nor look linked to it. It is kept only when it adds no crossed link or link through a class and grows the drawing by at most 10%.

The example spreads first, the way a person works. In the layouts, spreading comes after the single moves and leaf units, because that order measured better. The 15 graphs, cleaned up from the same starting drawings with half a second each; they start with 138 links through classes:

Single moves alone take links through classes from 138 to 57; all the steps together reach 36. Spreading first, as the worked example does, is worse than the order the layouts use.

VariantLinks through classes afterCrossed links after (465 before)Sharp crossings after (37 before)
All steps, as in the layouts3646210
Without region spreading4046110
Without group moves4046111
Without either4945711
Without leaf units5145110
Single moves only5745410
Spreading first, as in the example4846414

Most of the gain comes from the simplest step: single moves into open space alone take 138 links through classes down to 57. Leaf units, region spreading and group moves each add a little; spreading and group moves together remove about a quarter of what is left after the single moves and leaf units. None of the steps reduces crossings much. That is the layout's job; the clean-up mainly takes links off classes and opens sharp crossings.

The clean-up was taught by a person and turned into rules by an AI assistant

The clean-up was not designed from the literature, and it does not replay anyone's moves. Brendan Newlon, who works with these ontologies, taught it to an AI coding assistant, Claude (Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model). He solved the drawings by hand while saying what he was doing and why, named the principle behind each move, often with a metaphor (open space as a resource, a crowd pushed outward in pizza slices, a leaf that can always be solved), and suggested how a program could recognize the situation and carry the move out. The assistant's part was to distill that intuition into definitions, measures and steps a program can run, and to test whether each one held up on every graph, not only the one it was shown on. The loop had four parts.

  1. Showing and telling. In the Layout Lab, he tidied drawings by hand, typing what he was about to do and why before each move. The point was never the moves themselves, which only fit the graph they were made on, but the reasoning: what he looked at first, what he treated as a problem and what as harmless, which move he reached for and when he gave up on one. Within about ten minutes per ontology, this observed problem solving took links through classes to zero or one on PROV-O, telecom, the loan ontology and the 179-class bank, with crossings about level.
  2. From intuition to rules. The assistant turned each principle into something measurable: open space became a grid of empty cells, a crowd became the cells where problems pile up, "make room" became a push weighted by the room beyond each slice. Each rule was implemented and benchmarked on all the test graphs, and kept only if it helped across them. An early version came within a link or two of the hand-tidied drawings on every graph and beat them on several, but took 1 to 8 seconds.
  3. A walk-through to critique. The clean-up can replay its own steps in the Lab and in the Layout Playback, one stage at a time, drawing the open-space grid, the problem regions, the slices and the moved classes. Brendan critiqued each step the way a teacher marks a student's work ("why didn't the leaf go to the right, where there was room?"), and those critiques became the next rules. The finishing passes came from this step.
  4. Plain words both ways. He described strategies in his own terms (grid, density, open space, crowd, pizza slices, center of gravity). The assistant turned them into the definitions in the tabs above, and explained back, in the same plain terms, where a rule was slow or did not work. One example: "a push always looks worse at first; only the repairs after it make it pay off." He then refined the principle.

The principles Brendan taught, and what became of each:

Each principle the person taught became a specific rule in the clean-up.

The pattern, in Brendan's wordsWhat the clean-up does
Leaves, leaf chains and leaf triangles can always be solved. If one is crossed, a step was missed.Leaf units are turned around the class they hang from, and a last leaf pass runs at the end.
Look at the whole canvas first. Open space is a resource for solving problems.The open-space grid; candidate spots are open cells, not a fixed ring of positions.
Fix where problems pile up. A crowded region often causes many problems at once.Problems are counted per cell; the regions with the most come first.
Make room by pushing the crowd outward in slices toward open space, and push what lies beyond too.The slice push, weighted by the room beyond each slice and fading with distance.
Why spread a crowd with no problem in it? The layout is good, even if crowded.Only regions with problems are spread. An earlier version spread every dense region, and none of those spreads was kept.
A group move can make things worse before it makes them better.Spreads and group moves are judged after a few repair moves, not on their immediate effect.
Line length doesn't matter.The clean-up's cost has no length term.
Long labels are easier when the line to them runs sideways.A leaf with a long label tries sideways spots first.
Use the open space inside the drawing before making the canvas bigger.Growing the bounding box is costed (600 per doubling of area beyond the start).
Small nudges give a leaf clearance from a line; moving one end opens a sharp crossing.Nudges of 0.1 and 0.25 link lengths; sharp crossings and cramped classes are in the cost.
Don't fence me in: a leaf boxed in by lines should step out to the open side of its parent.A one-link class whose link still crosses something moves to the most open spot round its neighbor (fewest problems, then most room, then shortest link). From the playback.
Push the class off the line, even a curved one.A class a link runs through moves sideways just far enough, after the clean-up on straight links and after the routing on the drawn curves; kept only if better.
Shrink in from the canvas edge: a chain sprawling into empty canvas can fold up or down; groups with empty space between them can move closer. When time is short, the moves that make the canvas smaller come first.Pull-in: parts hanging by one link turn or draw in round their anchor, and whole groups slide toward the middle, edge-most first; kept only if the box shrinks (or links get much shorter) with no more problems. 9% less area on the development graphs, 27–29% on unseen ones.
A loop goes where nothing is.Self-link loops try 12 places round the class and take the emptiest.

Try it yourself. The Layout Lab and the Layout Playback are in this repository (Start Layout Lab.cmd, or tools/layout-bench/lab.html and playback.html). Readers can tidy drawings by hand, say why, and teach the layouts a principle we missed. The method is not specific to diagrams: any problem a person can look at and fix better than they can describe is a candidate. docs/SHOW-AND-TELL-LABS.md is a guide to the method and to building a lab of your own with an AI assistant, and docs/PLAYBACK-AND-LAB.md has the technical contract for adapting the two pages.

The lab, in this page. An edition of this write-up has the Layout Lab built in: ONTOLOGY-LAYOUT-ALGORITHMS-LAB.html. Pick any graph, tidy it by hand while typing why, run our clean-up on your drawing to compare, and download the whole session as one file for an AI assistant. It also has the sessions in which the clean-up was taught.

Two ideas from the sessions are not in the clean-up yet: curving links around hubs at the edge of the drawing (on the clinical record with three super-hubs), and pulling the classes of a loop closer together or untwisting a pair of classes.

Profiling the first version showed that the group moves took about 95% of its time and kept about one try in twenty. Two changes made the clean-up fast enough for the layouts: candidate spots come from the open-space grid (a few dozen instead of 96 fixed positions), and a class or problem that could not be improved is not tried again until something near it has moved.

New here: repairs chosen by readability counts, taught by a person; most single ingredients have precedents

Most single ingredients have precedents. What we have not seen elsewhere is the combination: repairs chosen and judged by readability counts after a layout, the regions picked by where those counts pile up, and the steps distilled from a person's explained problem solving. Readers may know closer prior work; we would welcome pointers.

  • Moving one class to a better spot to remove crossings is an established heuristic: Radermacher, Reichard, Rutter and Wagner (2018) move a vertex into its crossing-minimal region. The single moves here sample open cells instead of computing regions, and count links through classes and angles as well as crossings.
  • Turning what hangs off one class. Cut vertices and the parts of a graph they separate are classical (Hopcroft and Tarjan, 1973), and a tree hanging off one vertex can always be drawn without crossings. Using this as a repair after a layout, with the label-aware choice of side, is ours.
  • Spreading a region in slices. A push outward from a point that fades with distance resembles a local fisheye distortion (Sarkar and Brown, 1992), and evening out density resembles density-equalizing maps (Gastner and Newman, 2004). We have not seen it used this way: the point chosen from a count of readability problems after the layout, each slice weighted by the open space beyond it, and the push kept only if a few repair moves then make the drawing better.
  • Judged as graph drawing theory, nothing here is new: no new model, no bounds. The building blocks were chosen because they are the established best for the job, not as stand-ins for something to write from scratch. Stress placement is the standard for general undirected drawings and Pivot MDS its usual start. The new parts are applied: the clean-up and its passes, the routing joined to the placement, the work clock, and the evaluation against eleven libraries on graphs never seen during development.
  • Learning the procedure from a person. Interactive optimization with user hints is established (do Nascimento and Eades, 2005), but there the person guides one run. Here one person's principles, taught once, became a fixed procedure that runs without him on graphs he never saw. The lab that made this possible is offered as a tool of its own; see Try it yourself.

Link routing removes most remaining links through classes and shows every parallel link

The routing answers three gaps that a review pointed out for business ontologies: parallel and reciprocal links (Organization employs Person, Person manages Organization) drawn as straight lines lie exactly on top of each other; link names are not part of the drawing; and moving classes is the only way the layouts clear a link out of a class's way. The routing draws the links on the final positions and never moves a class:

  • Parallel links between the same two classes become arcs spread 24 px apart on both sides of the straight line (the middle one straight when their number is odd), so each one and its name can be seen.
  • Self-links become a loop on the corner of the class where the fewest links leave.
  • Bends: a link that runs through a class (or, when it pays off, crosses others) tries one bend at the corners and sides of the boxes in its way, gentle arcs to either side, and pairs of those bends; a bend is kept only if the drawing gets better counting crossings, links through classes and the extra length. Links through classes are routed first, then a second pass for any still in the way.
  • Ports: at a class with three or more links, link ends that would meet its box closer than 10 px apart are spread along the side they reach, in the same order, kept only if no link gets a new problem.
  • Names: each link's name goes at the point along its path where it covers no class, no other name and as few links as possible, longest names first.

Measured on the drawn curves, on Best Read's drawings before the refinements below (no class moved). Two margins. Here and in every table about the routing, a link counts as running through a class when it passes within 9 px of its box: closer than that, a drawn line with its arrowhead reads as touching the box, and the routing keeps that clearance. The rankings below count within 3 px, as published comparisons of layouts do, so the same drawing has more links through classes here. That, and the earlier drawings, is why Best Read's straight links show 61 links through classes on the 15 development graphs in this table and 39 in the rankings. The graphs carry no link names, so the names are made up: "has" plus the target class, "relatedTo" plus the target for a second link the same way, and so on; subclass links have none. Totals:

Routing the links leaves 15% fewer crossed links, two thirds fewer links through classes and 93% fewer names on a class or another name, and hides no parallel link, for about 10 bends per graph.

See it on any graph. Every drawing of ours in this page has a Curved links switch: it draws the links as the library does, with the routing, and gives the counts on the drawn links (3 px margin, as ranked). The switch is highlighted where curving removes problems or shows parallel links that straight lines hide; that is 58 of our 98 drawings (39 with fewer problems), and curving never adds a problem in these counts.

Over the 51 graphs: 15% fewer crossed links, two thirds fewer links through classes, no parallel link hidden (171 before), a fifth of the sharp crossings, half the crowded link ends and 93% fewer names on top of classes or other names, for about 10 bends per graph (a third of them the arcs of parallel links) and 2 to 4% more area. It takes at most 250 ms on the work clock, under 60 ms on most graphs. tools/layout-bench/routebench.mjs adds the steps one at a time.

Also tested for the review and not adopted: running the routing on the drawing before the clean-up instead of after it (twice the links through classes left, no smaller area: on these graphs the clean-up does not make the drawing sprawl); a smaller area penalty in the clean-up (half or a quarter: within 1% on crossings, a few links through classes fewer, up to 3% more area); a deeper look-ahead for group moves (8 repair moves, three tries instead of two: no clear gain, 6% more area on the development graphs); and giving the layout the names' widths so it reserves room for them (fewer names on names on the unseen graphs, but 15% more crossed links on the development graphs and up to 30% more area). tools/layout-bench/ekgbench.mjs runs these.

Watching the routing step by step led to four fixes

Watching the routing step by step showed four faults: loops took a fixed corner even where links left the class, names sat on top of the line, a bend could swing far outside the drawing, and some one-link classes ended fenced in by lines with open space nearby. Changes, each kept only where it measured better:

  • Loops on the open side. A self-link's loop now tries 12 places (four corners, and the middle and both ends of each side) and takes the one with the fewest links, classes and crossings in its wedge, counting the class's own links. On the five graphs with a self-link, four loops crossed a link before; none does now.
  • Names beside the line. A name can also sit just beside its link, on either side, where that covers less. Names on a class or another name 331 → 147, names with a link across them 1,330 → 882.
  • Bends stay inside the drawing. A bend that takes a link outside the box round the classes costs 1 per 20 px. Over 52 graphs, link length outside that box 2,817 → 1,056 px, for 15 more crossings (+0.8%), 3 fewer links through classes and 1.5% less area.
  • Classes moved off links. After the clean-up, three short passes (at most 120 ms of the work clock): two one-link classes of the same class trade places when that leaves fewer problems; a one-link class whose link still crosses or runs through something moves to the most open spot round its neighbor (fewest problems, then the most room, then the shorter link); a class that a link runs through, or passes within 9 px of, is pushed sideways off the line just far enough. After the routing, a class that a drawn curve still runs through is pushed off it the same way, the links are routed again, and the result is kept only if it has fewer problems. On straight links, links through classes 216 → 178.
  • Time limit. _ogSetTimeLimit(ms) sets the time the layouts, the clean-up and the routing may take, on the work clock (so still the same drawing on any computer). The default is 0.75 s since 12 November 2026; it was 1.5 s, and the tables in this write-up were measured at 1.5 s. The link routing keeps at least its time at 1.5 s, because it costs only about 25 ms and cutting it lost the most quality. Over the 51 test graphs, with two seeds each, 0.75 s made the drawings about 28% faster (mean 470 to 340 ms), and after routing they have 7% more crossed links and 14% fewer links through classes. 68 of the 102 drawings scored the same, 12 better and 22 worse, 6 of them by more than 15%, by a few crossings each.

The four fixes cut names on a class or name by more than half and links through classes by a fifth, for about 25 ms more per graph.

The drawings are 9% smaller on the development graphs and 27 to 29% smaller on the graphs never seen during development (23% over all 51), for as many problems: 6 fewer crossings, 6 more links through classes after routing (all on the two densest public ontologies, DOLCE and SAREF, where DOLCE also loses 5 crossings), and slightly more crowded names. Three graphs it was built for: Rome graph 7785, whose long chain ran off to the right, 2,026 → 1,677 px wide; the held-out deep taxonomy, 5,724 × 2,272 → 4,591 × 1,714 px (39% less area); the biomedical taxonomy's HormoneSignaling, 484 → 266 px from Signaling. Tried and not adopted: more room between groups (60 or 80 px: the same problems, less of the gain); not drawing in at all, only turning (most of the gain is from drawing in).

Area is 0 to 2% larger before pulling in. The slowest graph (SAREF, 98 classes and 160 links) takes about 1.6 s. Also tested and not adopted: starting the placement at the matching size, or at two or three times it, instead of five times too large. Over the 51 graphs and three seeds the four come within 0.5% of each other on crossed links, links through classes and sharp crossings together: the matching size has the most sharp crossings, twice the size the fewest links through classes but the most crossed links. That is the spread between seeds, not a gain, so five times stays. Trading two one-link classes' places alone rarely helps: where two of them lie on one ray from their neighbor, the far one's link runs through the near one whichever is farther.

Under a second per diagram; Graphviz is faster for large batches

One diagram. For a single ontology of up to 100 classes, Best Read takes about 0.3 to 0.5 s at the median and at most about 1.3 s, clean-up included, on a consumer laptop; Graphviz neato at general settings takes 20 to 50 ms. Below a second, the difference is not something a person opening one diagram will notice.

Many diagrams. It does add up for someone laying out many graphs in a batch. Our layouts stop at a fixed amount of work, so their time hardly grows with size: about 1.0 to 1.1 s each from 120 to 537 classes. On the same laptop:

  • 100 graphs of about 70 classes: about 1 minute with Best Read, about 5 seconds with neato at general settings.
  • 100 graphs of about 400 classes: about 2 minutes with Best Read, about 1.5 minutes with neato at general settings (8 to 15 minutes tuned), and hours with WebCola, which took 8 s to 3 minutes per graph, or ELK stress, 7 to 38 s per graph.

A computer half as fast takes twice as long and draws the same picture, up to 2.5 times slower; beyond that, the wait stays bounded and the drawing gets less work.

At 3,335 classes it does not: d3-force draws a fifth fewer crossings (60,264 against 75,127) and less than half the links through classes, and Graphviz sfdp did not finish within ten minutes in the browser. Our placement is single-level: at this size it gets few sweeps within its time limit, and the clean-up has no time left. At 1,204 classes four seconds take a fifth off the problems, mostly links through classes, and widen the lead; beyond that the returns shrink. At 3,335 classes extra time buys little and not steadily: at 6 s the placement packs the drawing five times tighter (area 3.4 against 16) and draws more crossings, and only at 60 s does the clean-up get far enough to bring the total 10% below the default run. Even then d3-force draws a fifth fewer problems in a seventh of the time. The limit is the single-level placement, not the time allowed: each sweep and each clean-up check costs more as the graph grows, so at this size the steps that matter get through only part of the graph. Above about 3,000 classes a multilevel placement is the fix, not a longer wait.

The first run at this size also found two faults, both fixed before the numbers above: the starting placement came out at an arbitrary scale and offset, and a class with a single link and no free spot near its neighbor was left where it started. Together they put part of the Cell Ontology a million pixels from the rest.

How the layouts work

Steps both layouts share

  1. Target distances. Every link gets a target length (170 px by default; subclass links slightly shorter; a link with a label is long enough for the label). The target distance between any two classes is the length of the shortest path of links between them.
  2. Placement. Classes are placed so that straight-line distances match the target distances as closely as possible (stress majorization), starting from a pivot-MDS placement, which gives the same result every time. Overlapping boxes are then pushed apart.
  3. Tidy-up. Four local searches run in this order. Each keeps a move only if it adds no crossing, no link through a box and no overlap:
    1. Swap two classes, or move one beside a neighbor, when that reduces crossings.
    2. Move a class off links that run through it.
    3. Pull classes toward their neighbors to shorten long links, then shrink the whole drawing evenly as far as the boxes allow.
    4. Move classes off links once more.
    Without these steps (placement alone, as in Graphviz neato) a drawing has typically 2–3× as many links through classes and about twice as many crossings.
  4. Leaf fanning, when used. Classes linked to a single other class are left out of placement and put back last.
    • Each is placed around its neighbor by trying 48 directions at the nearest free distances.
    • The chosen spot minimizes 100 × crossings + 80 × links touching the box + distance.
    • Each keeps at least max(40 px, label width + 16 px) from its neighbor, so the link's label fits.
    • Any whose link ends up crossed or touched is placed again.
    Ontologies have many classes of this kind, such as leaf subclasses.
  5. Clean-up. The drawing chosen is cleaned up as described under Clean-up after the layout.

Tidy Stress

Tidy Stress tries four settings of the shared steps within the time limit (0.75 s by default), scores each drawing, and keeps the most readable. The settings differ only in their options, not in the order of the steps:

  • random starts instead of the pivot-MDS start, keeping the start with the fewest crossings;
  • the pivot-MDS start, then moving any single-link class to a better free spot if there is one;
  • leaf fanning, with extra room round classes that have many links (the hub rings described below);
  • leaf fanning alone.

From 31 to 60 classes it tries three of these, and above 60 only the second, because sharing the time between settings leaves each too little time to tidy up.

Mycelium

  • Pods. Louvain community detection finds groups of closely linked classes. Links inside a group get 0.85× the target length and links between groups 1.6×, so placement separates the groups while still letting a class shared by two groups sit between them.
  • Hub rings. A link at a class with k neighbors is at least Σ(neighbor width + 20 px) / 2π long, the radius of a ring that holds all the neighbors side by side. On the clinical-record graph this rule alone cuts links through classes from about 80 to about 43.
  • Leaf fanning, as above.
  • Target length. 260 px from 100 classes.
  • Limits. It needs at least 8 classes and has a 1 s budget.

How readability is scored

Tidy Stress (between its settings) and Best Read (between the two layouts) choose the drawing with the lowest score. This score is how the layouts choose; it is not used to rank layouts on this page, because it has terms for link length. The score adds up:

  • 10 for every pair of crossed links;
  • 8 for every link that runs through a class box;
  • 2 for every pair of links that come within 30 px of each other;
  • 40 for every pair of overlapping boxes;
  • a tenth of the mean link length, plus a penalty when the mean exceeds 350 px;
  • a penalty for area beyond eight times the total area of the boxes, growing with the number of classes;
  • 25 for every multiple, beyond 1.8, of the median link length by which a link is longer.

The last two terms matter. A layout can avoid crossings by pushing classes far apart or by stretching a few links across the whole drawing. Without those terms, such drawings would win on crossings alone even though they are hard to read.

Best Read

  • Up to 30 classes: runs Tidy Stress's four settings and Mycelium, and keeps the lowest score.
  • 31 to 100 classes: runs Tidy Stress's settings for that size and Mycelium. For dense ontologies (more than two links per class) it runs only one Tidy Stress setting, so Mycelium has enough time.
  • Above 100 classes: runs Mycelium alone.

Its budget is the whole time limit up to 30 classes (0.75 s by default), 60% of it up to 100 classes and 40% above; the clean-up gets what is left.

for each link (u, v):
    len := L   (170 px; subclass links 0.9 L; Mycelium: L = 260 px from 100 classes)
    Mycelium:      len := max(len, min(3 L, ring(u), ring(v)))     ring(x) = Σ(neighbor width + 20) / 2π
                   len *= 0.85 inside a Louvain group, 1.6 between groups
    labeled link: len := max(len, (w_u + w_v)/2 + label width + 24)
D := all-pairs shortest-path lengths over len (Dijkstra)
place:  pivot-MDS start (+ random restarts while time allows) → stress majorization on D → push overlapping boxes apart
tidy:   fewer crossings → off links → shorten and shrink → off links   (each step time-boxed)
leaves: fan out round their neighbor → tidy once more → place again any that are crossed or touched
clean:  rounds of single moves → leaf units → region spreading → group moves, then a last leaf pass
        (within what is left of the time limit, at most a third of it)

Prior work these layouts use

Each layout combines established techniques with steps of its own. These are the established parts and where they come from. Our own parts are the tidy-up passes, the hub rings, the pod length factors, leaf fanning with room for labels, the readability score, the clean-up (see What is new here) and the settings, each chosen by benchmark.

The established techniques each layout builds on, and where they come from.

TechniqueSourceUsed for

Link lengths set by graph structureFor example Dwyer and others, WebCola, 2009 onwards; Noack, LinLog energy model, 2007The idea behind the pod lengths
Readability measuresPurchase, Which Aesthetic Has the Greatest Effect on Human Understanding?, 1997, and later workThe measures in the score
Moving one vertex to remove crossingsRadermacher, Reichard, Rutter and Wagner, A Geometric Heuristic for Rectilinear Crossing Minimization, ALENEX 2018The idea behind the single moves
